The Romanian DPA announced that on 28 October 2019 it finished an investigation into the courier company FAN Courier Express SRL. It found that the company had not implemented appropriate technical and organisational measures to secure personal data. Security incidents led to loss and unauthorised disclosure or access to personal data, including payment card and identity data, of about 1,100 people. The company was fined 52,325.9 lei, stated to be equivalent to EUR 11,000.
ICO issued a decision regarding access to third party personal data.

A data subject complained via the Polish DPA that the controller had not answered her access request under Article 15 GDPR within one month. The controller's letter and data file had never been sent because of a misconfigured security setting and a staff departure. The controller sent the data after the Commissioner's inquiry and changed its procedures. The Commissioner found a violation of Article 15, imposed a fine of EUR 8,000 and ordered further technical measures.
The HDPA rejected appeal filed by the Greek bank Eurobank Ergasias S.A. against HDPA's older decision linked to the exercise of the right to access and right to object under GDPR.

A member of parliament's scanned hospital access request form, sent only to the Military Hospital, appeared in news articles in February 2019. The authority found that the hospital did not notify the breach within 72 hours and did not record it in its breach register. It also found that the hospital had no internal incident-handling policy when the breach occurred, which meant inadequate organisational security measures. The authority imposed a fine of HUF 2,500,000 and ordered publication of the decision with the controller's identification data.

The 2019 annual report of the Baden-Württemberg data protection authority briefly describes a fine of EUR 100,000 imposed by notice of 24 October 2019 on a medium-sized food craft business. The company ran an online applicant portal on its website, but did not offer encrypted transmission and did not store the applicant data encrypted or password-protected. The applicant documents were also linked to Google, so anyone searching an applicant's name could open them without any access restriction. The authority found the company negligently failed to protect the data against access by unauthorised third parties. The report does not name the company or cite the GDPR articles for this case.
The Spanish DAP ordered Google to delist an article based on the "right to be forgotten".

The HDPA imposed a fine of EUR 20,000 and a reprimand to the telecommunication company Wind Hellas for violation of the GDPR and of the national law implementing the ePrivacy Directive and it issued a reprimand to the telephone services company ΠΛΕΓΜΑ ΝΕΤ for violation of the GDPR.
The UODO imposed the first fine on a public entity for unlawful processing of personal data in the Public Information Bulletin (BIP).
The UODO imposed a fine of ca €47,000 on a limited liability company ClickQuickNow Sp. z o. o. for preventing the exercise of the right to withdraw consent. Category:Article 5(1)(a) GDPR

The Romanian authority finished an investigation into Vodafone România on 15 October 2019. A petitioner had asked to stop receiving commercial messages and was told he was unsubscribed, but still received another unsolicited e-mail. The authority found breaches of Law no. 506/2004 (the ePrivacy law) and fined the company 10,000 lei. It also advised the company to respect the petitioner's request and recommended measures to send commercial messages only with prior express consent.

A former employee complained that, while he was on sick leave in May 2018, his employer reviewed and checked his company email account and office computer equipment, and photographed the results. The employer relied on the review for a later termination. The authority found that the employer had processed the complainant's personal data unfairly in reviewing his email account, had not properly informed him beforehand, and had breached the accountability principle by not taking adequate technical and organisational measures. It ordered the employer to review and delete the complainant's private data, to adopt internal rules and notices on monitoring, and imposed a fine of HUF 1,000,000 on its own initiative.

A fine of NOK 1,200,000 (approximately €120,000), reduced from NOK 2,000,000, was imposed against the Education Agency of the Municipality of Oslo due to breach of personal data security in the mobile application “Skolemelding”. The fine was issued due to the application's lack of security and subsequent violations of Article 32(1)(b) GDPR and Article 32(1)(d) GDPR and of the principle of accountability as foreseen in Article 5(2) GDPR read in conjunction with Article 5(1)(f) GDPR.
The DSB found an Article 32 GDPR violation where a dating platform did not require a double opt-in confirmation for email addresses used in the sign-up process.
The ANSPDCP finalised two investigations at Raiffeisen Bank S.A. and Vreau Credit S.R.L. and fined the two data controllers for violation of Article 32(1), (2) and (4) GDPR.

The Czech DPA issued a penalty order against a telemarketing company. Two people had objected to the processing of their data for direct marketing (one by email on 24 July 2018, the other repeatedly by phone), yet the company kept calling them. The company also ignored the Authority's call to remedy the situation. The Authority found a breach of Article 21(2) GDPR and imposed a fine of CZK 10,000. The order can be challenged by an objection within 8 days.
The HDPA re-examined complaints against the Greek internet and telecommunications service provider Forthnet.gr upon appeal and decided to reduce the fine it had previously imposed on it.

The Spanish DPA fined the airline Vueling €18,000 for relying on pre-checked consent boxes that enabled non-essential cookies and for continuing to use non-essential cookies even after users clicked "reject all."

A company running a home for seniors processed personal and health data of up to 55 clients without the legal authorisation required to provide social and health services. It also gave clients inadequate information about the processing and kept no records of processing activities. After an inspection by the Office, it was found guilty of three offences under the Czech data protection act. Under the absorption principle, a single fine of CZK 50,000 was imposed on the most serious offence, the breach of the lawfulness principle. The decision is a penalty order, against which an objection can be lodged within 8 days.

A person complained about the security cameras operated in the Kerepes town hall building, including the lack of prior information. The Authority extended the procedure ex officio to the municipality's general camera practice. It found that the camera surveillance breached the GDPR, that no information was given to data subjects before 26 March 2019, and that in the earlier period there was no designated controller, internal policy or privacy notice. It banned the unlawful camera processing and fined the municipality HUF 5,000,000, partly upholding the complaint. It also ordered publication of the decision and awarded the complainant HUF 10,000 for exceeding the procedural deadline.
The Rhineland-Palatinate DPA (LfDI) fined a local hospital € 105.000 due to its deficient organisational and structural personal data processing system.

Romania's data protection authority finished an investigation at Inteligo Media SA on 26 September 2019. On the avocatnet.ro website, the box for the daily 'Personal Update' email was left unticked, with text that the user ticks only to opt out, so users who did nothing were subscribed automatically. The company could not prove explicit consent for 4,357 users and relied on an inappropriate legal basis ('performance of a contract') for the daily email. The authority found breaches of Articles 5(1)(a) and (b), 6(1)(a) and 7 GDPR and imposed a fine of EUR 9,000.
The APD/GBA issued a warning because a controller did not delete personal data at request, following job application process.
The Belgian DPA (APD/GBA) fined € 10000 for requiring an ID to issue a new loyalty card, which violated the principle of data minimisation.
The Polish DPA (UODO) find the company Morele.net €660000 for violating the principle of data confidentiality and failing to ensure the security and confidentiality of personal data processed.

With the aim of ensuring the supremacy of EU law, the Portuguese DPA 'disapplied' several provisions of Portuguese Law 58/2019 in light of the GDPR's coming into force. It found that the disapplied articles jeopardised the application of the GDPR.

The DPA interpreted Article 44(2) of Law 58/2019 as conferring a discretionary power to assess, in cases where a GDPR violation is established, whether it is justified to depart from the legal rule of imposing a financial penalty on a given public body. The CNPD took the view that the waiver provided for in Article 44 can only be requested by public bodies and decided upon after notification of the accusation of an administrative offence, in the context of a specific administrative offence procedure.

The DVI director decided on 26 August 2019 to fine an online shop operator EUR 7,000. A person had repeatedly asked the company in 2018 to erase their data, including their mobile number, but the company kept sending commercial text messages to that number. The company also answered the person late, did not cooperate with the DVI, supplied information late and did not comply with the DVI's order. The company may appeal to court within ten working days.

A lawyer complained that the Swiss company N***Group AG, which runs a hotel booking website, had collected his name and email address when he asked for a holiday offer and then sent him newsletter advertising, without giving him the information required by Article 13 GDPR. The Austrian DSB upheld the complaint in part, finding that the company had not provided complete Article 13 information either at collection or by the end of the proceedings. It ordered the company to give the complainant the missing information within four weeks and to supplement its privacy statement; the rest of the complaint was dismissed. No fine was imposed. The decision is final.

The Swedish Data Protection Authority examined a trial in which a Skellefteå secondary school board used facial recognition cameras to record the attendance of 22 students over three weeks. The authority found that consent could not be a valid basis given the imbalance between students and the school, that no derogation under Article 9(2) applied to the biometric data, that the processing was more intrusive than necessary under Article 5, and that the impact assessment and prior consultation requirements of Articles 35 and 36 were not met. It imposed an administrative fine of SEK 200,000 and issued a warning about future use of facial recognition for attendance.

A former employee of a municipal public-space supervision service complained that an internal camera in the CCTV control room had monitored his work, that he was not informed in advance, and that the footage was used to end his public service employment. The authority partly upheld the complaint, finding unfair processing, no valid legal basis and inadequate information. It rejected the complainant's other requests, but ex officio banned the monitoring of control-room staff and ordered deletion of the stored footage. It also imposed a fine of HUF 1,500,000, and ordered the authority itself to pay the complainant HUF 10,000 for exceeding the procedural deadline.

In August 2019 the Berlin data protection commissioner imposed fines on Delivery Hero Germany GmbH totalling EUR 195,407, fees included. The fines were set in two notices, because some of the breaches fell under the data protection law in force before the GDPR; the press release gives no amount for each notice. Most of the cases concerned disregard of data subject rights: accounts of former customers were not deleted (ten cases), advertising emails were sent despite objections, and access requests were not answered or answered late (five cases). The authority concluded that the repeated breaches pointed to structural organisational problems. The new owner Takeaway.com accepted the notices and did not appeal, so the decision is final. The source is the commissioner's press release of 19 September 2019, not the notices themselves.

The Dutch DPA (AP) after investigation found multiple violations and decided to fine the Credit Registration Office (BKR) €830.000, because it charged fees for digital access requests and limited free access requests per mail to one per year. The BKR has announced they will appeal the fine. Additionally the BKR requested the AP does not publish their decision, but the Arhem court declined and the AP has published their decision.

A data subject complained that a tax advisory company gave her only a general access response under Art. 15 GDPR and refused to say which personal data categories it held about her. The authority found that the company violated her right of access by not providing any information on the specific data entries (categories such as names and tax-related details). It ordered the company, within two weeks under penalty of enforcement, to provide that information under Art. 15(1)(b). It rejected the complainant's request for a fine, because a data subject has no right to force the opening of administrative penalty proceedings. The complaint was otherwise dismissed. The parties later withdrew their appeals to the Federal Administrative Court, and the decision became final.

Two judges complained that the president of a regional court compiled a list of judges who were members of the Hungarian Judges' Association, taken from payroll membership-fee deductions and including tax IDs, and handed it out at a managers' meeting on 22 February 2019. The authority found the court unlawfully processed the data in breach of purpose limitation (Art. 5(1)(b)) and Art. 6 GDPR. It ordered the court to notify meeting participants that the data must be deleted, and imposed a fine of HUF 3,000,000 on its own initiative, rejecting the complainants' request for a fine as they had no standing on that point. The decision is to be published with the court's identifying data.

The Romanian authority concluded an investigation into LEGAL COMPANY & TAX HUB SRL. A set of files containing transaction details of people who had used a website was publicly accessible through two links between 10 December 2018 and 1 February 2019. The authority found the company had not implemented appropriate technical and organisational security measures. It fined the company 14,173.50 lei, equivalent to EUR 3,000.

The Romanian authority finished an investigation on 2 July 2019 into a hotel operator, World Trade Center Bucharest. A printed breakfast check-in list with personal data of 46 guests was photographed by unauthorised outsiders and the data was published online. The authority found a breach of Article 32 GDPR, because the controller had not made sure staff only process data on its instructions and had not applied adequate technical and organisational measures. It imposed a fine of 71,028 lei, equal to EUR 15,000. The investigation began after the controller's own breach notification.

ANSPDCP announced its first fine under the GDPR, against UniCredit Bank S.A., after an investigation concluded on 27 June 2019. The bank had not applied adequate technical and organisational measures (data protection by design, data minimisation), so transaction detail documents made available online to payment beneficiaries disclosed the payer's national ID number (CNP) and address. 337,042 data subjects were affected between 25 May 2018 and 10 December 2018. The bank was fined RON 613,912, equivalent to EUR 130,000.

A debtor asked a lender to delete his phone numbers after withdrawing consent. The lender refused, relying on legitimate interest and a restriction of processing for a narrow purpose. The authority found the processing had no legal basis and breached purpose limitation, data minimisation and the right to erasure. It ordered deletion of the numbers and proof of this within 30 days. It also fined the company HUF 1,000,000 on its own initiative. It granted business-secret treatment for some documents but refused it for the balancing test.

A police officer lost a private, unprotected USB stick holding personal data of the force's whole staff of about 1,733 people (birth data, mother's name, social security number, post). The police headquarters learned of the loss on 11 January 2019 but only notified the authority by post on 25 February 2019, well beyond the 72 hours. The authority found a breach of Article 33(1) GDPR, fined the headquarters HUF 5,000,000, ordered it to take measures so future breaches are notified on time, and ordered publication of the decision with the controller's identity.

After the hospital reported a data breach in which many staff unlawfully looked at the medical file of a well-known Dutch person, the AP investigated access to patient files. It found that since January 2018 the hospital had not used two-factor authentication and had not regularly reviewed access logs, breaching the security duty in Article 32(1) GDPR. The AP fined the hospital EUR 460,000 and ordered it, under a penalty payment, to fix both gaps within fifteen weeks. The AP's later web page says the Hague court reduced the fine to EUR 350,000 and that this ruling is final.

A complainant asked a company to delete her personal data (name, date of birth, address, business information) from its website, after objecting on 17 March and 1 April 2019. She no longer carried out business, as her trade licence was suspended. The company ignored both requests and the Office's call to remedy the situation, and the data was still online on 3 June 2019. The Office issued a penalty order finding a breach of the right to erasure under Article 17(1) GDPR and fined the company CZK 10,000.

A news article reports that the Spanish data protection authority fined LaLiga EUR 250,000 over its mobile app, which could remotely activate users' phone microphones to detect bars showing football without paying. The AEPD found the information given to users opaque and held that users must be informed each time the microphone is activated, not only at installation. It also found a breach of the requirement that consent can be withdrawn at any time. The authority gave LaLiga one month to correct the app. LaLiga disputes the findings and says it will appeal in court.

Two complainants objected that a company had bought their bank loan debt and their personal data without holding the licence required for debt purchasing. The Hungarian central bank (MNB) had already found that the company carried out debt purchasing without authorisation. NAIH found that the company processed the complainants' data without a proper legal basis and for an unlawful purpose, in breach of Articles 5(1)(a)-(b) and 6(1) GDPR. It restricted the processing, banned use of the data for debt management, and on its own initiative imposed a fine of HUF 1,000,000. It rejected the complainants' request for a fine, since they are not parties to that measure.

The French DPA (CNIL) held that using an unprotected URL address to share documents containing personal data violates Article 32 GDPR. Retaining personal data of an applicant for a lease after another applicant has been selected also violates Article 5(1)(e) GDPR.

The authority investigated, on its own initiative, the entry procedure at festivals run by Sziget, where visitors' ID documents were scanned and photos and recordings taken. For 2016 to 24 May 2018 (Infotv.) it found no proper legal basis, breach of purpose limitation and inadequate prior information, but imposed no fine because the company was an SME and the practice had ended. For the period from 25 May 2018 (GDPR) it found an invalid legal basis and breaches of purpose limitation and data minimisation. It fined the company HUF 30,000,000, ordered it to bring its practice into line with the GDPR and ordered publication of the decision.

A staff member of a social and child welfare institution mistakenly posted nine documents containing personal data of 18 people, including minors, to another social institution. The institution notified the authority only 16 days after its stated awareness date (24 days after the authority's view of when it learned of it), far beyond the 72-hour limit. The authority found a breach of Article 33(1) GDPR, imposed the minimum fine of HUF 100,000, ordered measures to ensure timely notification of future breaches, and ordered publication of the decision with the controller's identity.

A police officer used his official user ID to query vehicle holder data for the licence plate of a private acquaintance, then used a SARS request to the Bundesnetzagentur to obtain her phone numbers. He called her without any official reason or her consent. The Baden-Württemberg DPA fined him EUR 1,400 by notice of 9 May 2019, reported as the first fine against a public-sector employee under the GDPR and the new state law. The press release says the fine is final and that the public-body fine exemption did not apply because the conduct was private and not attributable to his employer.

The DPA fined a controller €107,000 for repeatedly sending unsolicited marketing communications without the data subject's consent. The controller bore liability even though it was a third-party who sent the communications using their own database.

The complainant was refused a subscription contract because Respondent 1 said he had unpaid debts from earlier contracts, which it had assigned to Respondent 2. The contracts had been transferred into his name by phone by a person using his birth data and ID number but giving different mothers' names. Respondent 1 wrongly told him it no longer held his data and refused access, and it kept four different mother's names for him. Respondent 2 processed his data on the wrong legal basis (contract performance). The Authority found breaches of access, transparency, accuracy and accountability by Respondent 1 and of legal basis and accountability by Respondent 2. It fined them HUF 2,000,000 and HUF 1,000,000, ordered them to prove a legitimate interest or stop, restricted processing in the meantime, and rejected the requests for erasure and a processing ban.

An employee asked his employer, a public university, for access to his personal data (insurance reporting, tax paid, gaps, job descriptions). The university did not answer within one month, did not extend the deadline or give reasons, and only replied after the authority opened proceedings, and then incompletely. The authority found breaches of Articles 12(3)-(4) and 15(1) GDPR, ordered the university to fulfil the request within 8 days, fined it HUF 600,000, rejected the claim for compensation (a court matter) and ordered publication of the decision.

After a 2017 breach of the Rousseau platform and Movimento 5 Stelle websites, the Garante had prescribed security measures in December 2017. It checked compliance with an inspection in November 2018 and found gaps: incomplete logging of database access, shared administrator credentials, outdated systems and issues with e-voting data. It ordered the Movimento 5 Stelle Association and the Rousseau Association to fix these within set deadlines and run a data protection impact assessment of e-voting. It fined the Rousseau Association, as processor, EUR 50,000 for breaching Article 32 GDPR.

Category:Article 4(1) GDPR Category:2019 The President of the Personal Data Protection Office in Poland (UODO) imposed the first fine in the amount of over PLN 943 000 for the failure to fulfil the information obligation.
Portuguese DPA rules that not posting signage about CCTV footage collection in covered areas represents a breach of the controller's information duties under article 13 GDPR

The Danish Data Protection Authority inspected taxi company Taxa 4x35 in autumn 2018 and found that customer trip records were kept too long. Customer names were deleted after two years but phone numbers, which link trips to a person, were kept for five years, leaving 8,873,333 identifiable trip records older than two years. The authority reported the company to the police and proposed a fine of DKK 1.2 million. The Copenhagen City Court (byret) imposed DKK 100,000 and the High Court (landsret) increased it to DKK 250,000.

Files listing usernames and passwords for over 35,000 users of Bergen municipality's school login system (eFeide) were openly accessible to pupils. A pupil used an administrator login to access pupil and staff data and sent messages from a headteacher's account. The municipality had not set up two-factor authentication despite knowing it was needed. The Norwegian Data Protection Authority ordered two-factor authentication for staff logins and fined the municipality NOK 1,600,000 for inadequate security under Articles 5(1)(f) and 32(1)(a) and (b) GDPR.

A borrower under a car-financing loan asked the controller to delete his telephone number and to correct his address. The controller refused to delete the number, relying on legitimate interest, but its balancing test was inadequate and did not cover each purpose separately. The authority found that the phone number was processed without a legal basis and in breach of purpose limitation and data minimisation. It also found that the controller had not informed the complainant of processing for a different purpose. It ordered deletion of the number and imposed a fine of HUF 1,000,000. The rectification complaint was dismissed because asking for proof of a new address is acceptable.

The Hungarian authority examined a personal data breach reported by the Kecskemét city mayor's office. The office had sent the full, unredacted whistleblower report of a former employee to the employer institution, which then dismissed the employee partly on the basis of that report. The authority found that this disclosure had no legal basis under the GDPR and breached Article 5(1)(a) and Article 6, and did not find a breach of the breach notification and communication duties in Articles 33-34. It imposed a fine of HUF 1,000,000 and ordered publication of the decision naming the controller.

A law firm article reports that Malta's data protection commissioner fined the Lands Authority EUR 5,000 on 18 February 2019. The Authority's website lacked appropriate security measures, so over 10 GB of personal data, mostly sensitive and including correspondence with individuals, could be found through a simple Google search. The Authority did not appeal and has begun penetration testing and moved its data to servers run by the Malta Information Technology Agency. The article is a secondary commentary, not the decision itself, and cites no GDPR articles.
Portuguese DPA rules that phone call recordings must be made available to the data subject upon his/her request under article 15 GDPR.

The UK DPA (ICO) fined Leave.EU, the Brexit campaign group, and Eldon Insurance, an insurance company, a total of approximately €140,900 (GBP 120,000) for serious breaches of the PECR and sending nearly 300,000 emails to Eldon customers with a Leave.EU newsletter.

The CNIL's restricted committee fined the company (anonymised as 'société X', identified in Fino as Google LLC) EUR 50 million. Two collective complaints by NOYB and La Quadrature du Net, covering 9,974 people, led to an online inspection of the account creation flow when setting up an Android device. The committee found that the company was not its main establishment in the EU, so the CNIL was competent, and found failures in the legal basis for ad personalisation processing and in the accessibility and clarity of the information given to users. It also ordered publication of the decision.

This is a law firm's news article, not the decision itself. A patient complained that a State Hospital did not satisfy her request for access to her medical file because the file could not be located. After investigating, the Cypriot Commissioner imposed an administrative fine of EUR 5,000 on the hospital. The article also reports a separate EUR 10,000 fine on a newspaper for publishing the names and pictures of police officers; that case is not part of this record.

A law firm's news article reports two separate decisions of the Cyprus data protection Commissioner. One fined a State Hospital EUR 5,000 for failing to satisfy a patient's access request because her medical file could not be located. In the other, a newspaper was fined EUR 10,000 for publishing, in print and online, the names and pictures of two police officers, and a photograph of a third. The Commissioner held that the aim could be reached with initials, blurred faces or distant photographs, and weighed EU Court of Justice case law on freedom of expression versus privacy.

In March 2019 a complaint alerted the Hamburg authority that Facebook Germany GmbH had not notified it of a data protection officer. The previous officer had stepped down in 2017 and no replacement was reported, although a team in Ireland had in practice been designated. Facebook raised legal doubts about whether this was a fineable breach. The authority said open legal questions cannot justify inaction and fined Facebook Germany GmbH EUR 51,000 for breaching the duty to communicate the DPO's contact details. It took into account that the breach was negligent, was ended at once, and that a DPO had been in place throughout.

In 2018 a software update left a security hole in the HVV customer portal. A logged-in customer could change the URL and see other customers' order history, invoices and bank data. The HVV learned of the hole on 6 July 2018 but did not report it to the Hamburg authority within 72 hours; the authority heard of it on 11 July 2018 from a call by another company. The HVV also failed to notify the affected people in time and wrongly relied on an exemption. The authority did not accept the HVV's explanations and imposed a final fine of EUR 20,000 for the late notification to the authority and the late notification of data subjects.

The Hamburg data protection authority ran fine proceedings against Hamburger Volksbank eG. The bank sent a customer an advertising newsletter by email although the customer had expressly objected to direct marketing. The bank admitted the breach and blamed a processing error by one employee. The authority imposed a fine in the mid four-figure range under Art. 83(5)(b) GDPR for breaching Art. 21(2),(3) GDPR. The report gives no exact amount. The bank accepted the fine and did not appeal.

The Brandenburg data protection authority's 2019 annual report describes a fine against an unnamed company. The company first contacted people who had made access requests only in English, although it addressed the German market. It also failed to conclude a proper written processing contract. The authority found negligent breaches of Art. 12 and 28(9) GDPR in connection with the right of access (Art. 15). It imposed a total fine of EUR 50,000, taking the company's cooperation in the fine proceedings into account as a mitigating factor. The beginning of the case description is missing from the excerpt, so the full facts are not visible.

The Bavarian authority's 2020 annual report describes its first fine notice issued after the GDPR began to apply, issued in 2019. A company had refused the authority access to its business premises and data processing systems during an unannounced on-site inspection under Art. 58(1)(f) GDPR. The company objected and the case went to the local court. The court agreed with the authority's reasoning but reduced the fine from EUR 20,000 to EUR 7,000, citing among other things the considerable time elapsed since the violation at the end of 2018.
The Commissioner fined a doctor € 14,000 for publishing sensitive patient data on Instagram.

This is the 2019 annual report of the Saxon data protection commissioner. In the chapter on administrative offence proceedings in the non-public sector, it says that 12 fines were imposed in 2019. One of them was a fine of EUR 500 for breaching the duty to give a data subject access to their data (Art. 15 GDPR). The other eleven fines (EUR 50 to 800) concerned unlawful dashcam operation. The report gives no name for the fined party and no day for the decision.

This is the 2019 activity report of the Saxon data protection commissioner, not a single decision. In the private sector the authority closed 33 administrative offence cases and set 12 fines. One was EUR 500 for failing to answer a data subject's access request (Art. 15 GDPR). Eleven were between EUR 50 and 800 for unlawful dashcam use (8 under Art. 6 GDPR, 3 old cases under § 43 BDSG). In the public sector, 7 fines totalling EUR 5,950 were imposed, all on police officers under the old Saxon data protection act, and none under the GDPR.

A heise online article reports that the Hamburg data protection authority issued a fine notice on 17 December 2018 against a small mail-order company. The company let a postal service intermediary process customer data without a data processing agreement and refused, even after advice from the Hessian authority, to draw one up. Hamburg found a breach of Art. 28(3) GDPR and set a fine of EUR 5,000 plus EUR 250 fees, treating the conduct as intentional. The company's representative said he would object to the notice.

The Baden-Württemberg data protection authority fined a social media provider EUR 20,000 for breaching data security under Art. 32 GDPR. The company reported a hack in which data of about 330,000 users, including passwords and email addresses, was stolen and later published. The authority found that the company had knowingly stored user passwords in plain text. The fine was kept low because of the company's exemplary cooperation, transparency and rapid security improvements, and because the total financial burden on the company was taken into account.
Portuguese DPA determines generalized access to patient records within a hospital breaches the minimization, integrity and confidentiality principles.

The DSB fined a betting store € 5.280 for video surveillance (CCTV) that was recording a wide area in front of the location, without protocols of the usage, without deletion within 72 hours and without public marking of the video surveillance.

On 31 July 2018 the Dutch DPA ordered UWV, the Dutch employee insurance agency, to bring the security of its employer portal up to standard by 31 October 2019, under a penalty: EUR 150,000 a month, at most EUR 900,000, if it had not done so by then. This is an order under penalty payments, not a fine. The deadline was later extended once, to 1 March 2020; in June 2020 the AP found the security improved and said UWV did not have to pay the penalty.

The DSB found that a fee of €30 for a copy of historic bank transaction data, that is not available via online banking anymore, violates the right to access under Article 15 GDPR. GDPR is also applicable to cases that were brought under Directive 95/46 but were pending before the DPA on 25. 5. 2018.

On 25 May 2018, the day the GDPR began to apply, the European Data Protection Board endorsed 16 documents of its predecessor, the Article 29 Working Party. They are the guidelines on consent, transparency, automated decision-making and profiling, personal data breach notification, data portability, data protection impact assessments, data protection officers, the lead supervisory authority and administrative fines, a position paper on the exemptions from keeping records of processing, and papers on binding corporate rules and on adequacy. It is a Board document, not a fine.

Category:Article 12(5) GDPR The DSB issued a decision related to the righ to be forgotten: to exercise this right, the controller may not require more data than the ones previously asked to the data subject.
The Spanish DPA closed a procedure against the proprietor of a false camera installed in a public space because they did not process any personal data.

The Spanish Data Protection Agency (AEPD) decided not to take further actions on Google, LLC (Google Spain, S.L.) and Facebook Spain, S.L. as data controllers for the non-compliance with the right to be forgotten of a Spanish citizen, as per Article 17 GDPR.

The Spanish DPA referred a case to the Irish DPA regarding Facebook transfers of data to third parties. The Irish DPA rejected the case, since Ireland has not implemented Article 80(2) GDPR and the consumer organisation that brought the claim in Spain could therefore not act without an individual mandate.

The Spanish DPA found that an access request was abusive, taking into account the context and the background of the relationship between the data subject and the controller. The data subject had previously filed various claims and lawsuits against the controller in other fields of law.
The Spanish DPA considered that the use of drones by the municipality of Fuenlabrada (Spain) for vehicle traffic control purposes was compliant with GDPR.

The Spanish DPA was not able to launch a sanction procedure because the ICO did not send any information following their cooperation request in the IMI, despite having accepted the case. After Brexit, the Spanish authority decided to archive the case.

The Spanish DPA held that the monitoring of news and social networks by the Directorate for National Security and the Spanish police forces did not violate any data protection regulation, since no personal data had been processed.

The Spanish DPA confirmed that the use of a thermal camera by private security guards to detect individuals' temperatures does does not fall under the scope of the GDPR when there is no further processing of the data shown by the camera, and the persons are not asked to identify themselves.

The Spanish DPA concluded that the use of a thermal camera to verify if users of a service have a higher temperature than a certain threshold, in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic, does not fall under the scope of the GDPR when there is no further storing, processing or any operation on the data shown by the camera, and the persons are not asked to identify themselves.
The Spanish Data Protection Agency (AEPD) decided not to take further actions on Telefónica as data controller for a possible personal data breach affecting confidentiality, as per Article 32 GDPR.

The Spanish DPA decided not to fine a football club that suffered a data breach because it had implemented adequate security measures and was diligent in mitigating the breach's consequences and reporting it to the authority.

The Spanish DPA considered that the software developer of the interactive, real-location game 'Pokemon Go', had implemented adequate measures to mitigate the risks stemming from the fact malicious users could fake their location, and misuse the location data of other users.
The Spanish DPA established that the parameters of a productivity calculation is not personal data and is therefore not subject to the right to rectification.
The Spanish DPA ordered a controller to comply with a data subject's access request, either by providing the requested information or by explaining why it did not comply with the request.
The Spanish DPA dismissed a complaint about the use of surveillance camera in public spaces. The equipment was never put into use, so there was no processing of personal data.

The Spanish DPA sanctioned a processor for violating GDPR Articles 28(2) and 28(3). This was despite the fact that no written contract existed between the processor and the subprocessors and the controller had not been told of the subprocessors' involvement in data processing activities.

The Spanish DPA handled a personal data breach notified by the Fundación Sociedad Científica de Oncología Médica (FSOM), the foundation behind the study, after a cyber incident at its processor, a CRO, affected study participants' contact and health data. The DPA found that the controller lacked appropriate technical and organisational measures, and proposed a fine of EUR 70,000 under Article 5(1)(f) GDPR. The controller admitted liability, paid voluntarily and waived administrative appeals, so two cumulative 20% reductions brought the fine to EUR 42,000, and it was ordered to demonstrate the measures within three months.

The DPA fined Vodafone €1,050,000 for the failure to implement adequate security measures, allowing the unlawful registration of an additional phone line and the disclosure of duplicate invoices to third parties.
The DPA fined a security provider €100,000 for deterring data subjects from exercising their rights by referring them to a premium-rate phone number, in violation of Article 12(2) GDPR.

The DPA held that a municipality violated the principle of confidentiality after examination papers from an employment-training were disposed in the general waste instead of being destroyed. This allowed for access to the information by third parties.

A former employee complained that his employer had installed cameras that record sound as well as images in work areas, and that the recordings were the sole basis for a disciplinary dismissal procedure. The company confirmed that the system records audio and said this was needed because of a burglary and to document its dispute with the employee. The AEPD held that recording audio in the workplace is intrusive and disproportionate, because testimony from colleagues or the video images alone would have been enough. It fined the company EUR 4,000 for breaching the data minimisation principle (Article 5(1)(c) GDPR) and ordered it to disable the audio mode within one month. The company filed no submissions, so the initiation agreement was treated as the resolution proposal.

A Dutch complainant asked Michael Page, part of PageGroup, for access to her data and was first asked for excessive identity documents. The Dutch authority transferred the complaint to the AEPD as lead authority. The AEPD found that the rights-handling procedure run by the Spanish entity PAGE GROUP EUROPE, S.L. breached Article 12 and the data minimisation principle of Article 5(1)(c) GDPR, and proposed fines of EUR 50,000 and EUR 250,000. The company paid EUR 240,000 voluntarily with the 20% reduction, so the proceedings were declared terminated. No further measures were ordered because the company had adopted a new procedure.

The Spanish Data Protection Agency (AEPD) decided not to take further actions on Sound Soul, S.L. as data controller for the possible non-compliance with the data minimisation principle, as per Article 5(1)(c) GDPR.

This is a warning (advertencia) about processing that was only planned: the AEPD did not find a breach and imposed no fine. On 6 January 2026 the Spanish data protection authority (AEPD) received a written report that a company was introducing an AI tool to screen and score job candidates and staff applying for internal moves: it analyses CVs, gives scores and ranks candidates. The tool was not yet in use in Spain, and the company's name is blacked out in the published text. The company had told staff representatives that the tool only supports the process and that the final decision is always human. The AEPD issued the warning under Article 58(2)(a) GDPR and told the company to build in data protection by design and by default (Arts. 24 and 25), to assess the risks and, if the processing is likely to be high risk, to carry out a data protection impact assessment before it starts (Art. 35), to be transparent towards candidates and workers (Arts. 12 to 14), and to assess whether Article 22 (decisions based only on automated processing) applies. On that last point the AEPD said that human involvement must be effective: the person must be able to assess the score critically and decide without the decision being determined in fact by the automated result, and whether Article 22 applies depends on how the decision process actually works. The AEPD added that failing to adopt the necessary measures could lead to an investigation and corrective action, including sanctions.
The Spanish DPA (AEPD) fined €5,000 (reduced to €3,000) Abanca Corporación Bancaria for using unnecessary cookies on their website before obtaining the consent of the user.

The AEPD issued a reprimand to the Ministry of internal affairs due to their misuse of surveillance cameras in a police station. The controller did not inform about the specific purposes of the surveillances cameras which were used for the employees' monitoring and, thus, breached the principle of purpose limitation.
The Spanish DPA (AEPD) imposed a warning on an association for the protection of prison workers for publishing personal data without consent on Twitter.
The Spanish Data Protection Agency sanctioned the Municipality of El Espinar with a warning for violating GDPR by publicly disclosing personal data in electoral board lists.

The Spanish DPA held that where an employee had signed an image rights transfer agreement with their employer, prior to the display of an advertisement banner using the employee's image, this could be considered as a legal basis for data processing.

The AEPD issued a reprimand to the Directorate-General of the Spanish Civil Guard for a lack of transparency. The data controller did not provide information to the data subjects who filled out the travel permit form with their personal data, as required by Article 13 GDPR.

The Spanish DPA (AEDP) fined FURNISHYOURSPACE SL €3,000 for infringing the Spanish Law regulating cookies after an investigation launched due to a complaint referred by the Berlin DPA, for offering unclear information and not giving the option of rejecting the cookies.
The Spanish DPA issued a warning to Iberia Líneas Aéreas de España for not informing their workers in accordance with Article 13 GDPR regarding a fingerprint clock-in system.
The Spanish DPA (AEPD) issued a warning to a pub for recording and disseminating the image of its customers on their social networks without a legal basis.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) decided to early finish the sanction procedure against the company Bodegas Dinastía, S.L. (the defendant) for the infringement of its information duties related to cookies, as per Article 22(2) of the Spanish Law on Information Society Services (LSSI) — amongst others, the Spanish law regulating cookies — and Article 13 of the GDPR. The defendant agreed to an early settlement of the case by paying a reduced fine (1,600 €) out of the total envisaged by the AEPD in case of ascertained violation (2,000 €).
The Spanish DPA (AEPD) warned a Home Owners' Association for an infringement of Article 5(1)(f) GDPR, due to the disclosing of personal data in a debtors list.

The Agencia Española de Protección de Datos filed a case brought by ms. A.A.A against mr. B.B.B in which the applicant denounced that the respondent had installed a video surveillance system with an alleged focus on the complainant's house, infringing article 5(3) GDPR which enshrines the principle of data minimisation.
The Spanish DPA (AEPD) fined Telefónica €15,000 for failing to respond to a customer's objection under Article 21 GDPR, who asked several times to stop receiving advertising e-mails.
The Spanish DPA (AEPD) closed a procedure against a website after verifying that it only automatically installed necessary cookies without users’ consent.
The AEPD warned the Asturian Handball Federation for not having appointed a DPO and not having complied with Article 13 GDPR.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) decided to impose a fine up to €30,000 on Twitter International Company (Twitter Spain, S.L.) for the infringement of its information duties related to cookies, as per Article 22(2) of the Spanish Law on Information Society Services (LSSI) —this is the Spanish law regulating cookies, connected to Article 13 GDPR.

The Spanish DPA fined Orange €50,000 (reduced to €30,000) for processing personal data without a valid legal basis, since processing was based on a fraudulent telephone portability contract. The DPA stated that Orange did not have an adequate identity verification system for portability requests.
The Spanish DPA issued a reprimand against the municipality of Ayuntamiento de Molina de Segura for lacking a DPO.
The Spanish DPA (AEPD) issued a warning to the city Council of Burgos for not having appointed a data protection officer, thus breaching Article 37 GDPR.
The Spanish DPA issued a warning to the former worker of a business that processed personal data of their clients from a previous employment relationship without any legitimate basis.

The claimant filed a complaint with the AEPD against the political party Partido Socialista Obrero Español (PSOE) for failing respect his right to object to the processing of information as they sent him political advertisement by email.

A father complained that the RFEF, when registering his minor daughter (a foreign national born and raised in Spain) as a player, asked for a detailed school record on top of the documents FIFA requires. The AEPD found a breach of the data minimisation principle in Article 5(1)(c) GDPR. It imposed a fine of EUR 100,000 and ordered the RFEF to bring its processing of such registrations into line with the principle within two months. The resolution becomes enforceable only after the appeal period for administrative review expires.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) found that the Regionalist Party of Aragon (PAR) violated Article 21 GDPR by continuing to send an individual unsolicited political canvassing materials after she had exercised her right to reject.
The AEPD found that the Socialist Party of Catalonia (PSC-PSOE) violated Article 21 GDPR due to unsolicited political propaganda sent after the data subject exercised his right to object.
The Spanish DPA warned a City Council for infringing the integrity and confidentiality principle by publishing personal data related to a public grant procedure.

The AEPD issued a reprimand to the Spanish far-right political party VOX. The data controller had sent an email without blind copying, to the members of that political party, infringing Article 5(1)(f) GDPR (integrity and confidentiality principle).
The Spanish DPA (AEPD) warned a Municipality for failing to meet its information obligations to its employees regarding the placement of video surveillance cameras that also record audio.
The Spanish DPA fined a website €3000 for installing third-party cookies without the user's consent, as well as for not informing the user about the purpose of such cookies.

The APED fined 2.500 € a data controller for sending advertisement email without blind carbon copy (Bcc) the email recipients. By disclosing the email addresses of the recipient, the company violated the principle of integrity and confidentiality – Article 5(1)(f) GDPR-.
The Spanish DPA issued a warning to a minor that recorded a video while assaulting another minor, together with a group of others, and subsequently posted it on Instagram.
The AEPD issued a Spanish City Council with a warning of an infringement of Article 5(1)(c) pursuant to Article 83(5) over installed surveillance cameras in the City Hall.

The Spanish Data Protection Agency (AEPD) decided to impose a minor warning on a Spanish citizen (the defendant) for the non-adequate installation of a video surveillance system allegedly pointing to the common swimming pool of the housing association, and the consequent infringement of the data minimisation principle related, as per Article 5(1)(c) GDPR.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) issued a reprimand to a Spanish religious brotherhood (sacramental y penitencial cofradía de nuestro padre jesús sacramentado y maría santísima de la piedad, amparo de los leoneses) for unlawfully processing personal data of its members.
The Spanish DPA held that, for an access request to be valid, it should be done through the appropriate channel (in this case, the DPO), and should be properly documented.
The Spanish DPA (AEPD) admitted a claim against the Asturias Healthcare System for not attending a data subject's access request to medical data.

The Spanish DPA decided that, in light of an access request, the controller needs to inform the data subject about whether it has transferred their data to third parties and to whom, even if the controller does not hold any data itself.

The Spanish DPA decided to archive a 'right to be forgotten' case, stating that the data subject did not have any interests which overrode the rights to freedom of speech and information of the newspaper. The search result that the data subject wished to de-list was of public relevance, was not obsolete, and was not proven to be incorrect.

The AEPD received a complaint from a citizen who tried to exercise the right to erasure pursuant to Article 17 GDPR. The controller did not respond to the request. As such, the AEDP notified the controller of responding within ten business days with either a confirmation of the data being deleted or a reasoning for not deleting the data.

The DPA held that automatically refusing to disclose the identity of persons who accessed medical records was incompatible with the enhanced transparency required in the healthcare context, in violation of Article 15 GDPR. It ordered the controller to grant access or provide a properly reasoned refusal.

A complainant and relatives were required by their bank's branch to hand over a full notarial inheritance deed, including information about third parties, to process the estate of a deceased account co-holder. The AEPD found that CaixaBank breached data protection by design (Art. 25 GDPR) and failed to give Art. 13 information. It proposed fines of EUR 500,000 and EUR 10,000 and closed the Art. 30 charge. CaixaBank paid voluntarily, without admitting liability, and obtained a 20% reduction, so the final fine was EUR 408,000. The AEPD ended the procedure and ordered corrective measures within six months.
The DPA found that a public authority’s mobile app collected more personal data than necessary, including IP addresses and device data, in violation of principle of data minimisation.
The Romanian DPA fined a medical clinic approximately €2.000 after it unlawfully processed and disclosed a patient's health data to another controller.

The DPA fined a public-sector group €5,250 for unlawfully disclosing an employee's audio recording to recipients that were in copy of the access request. The controller should have ensured the data subject intended to provide the recording to such recipients.

The Croatian Personal Data Protection Agency (AZOP) has decided that Raiffeisen bank was in violation of the GDPR by asking its clients to pay approx. 200 HRK (approx. 30 EUR) for delivering documentation regarding a home loan. The client needed it to initiate proceedings for reimbursement of overcharged debt. The Bank says it will not give up its current practice.
The AEPD fined a gas distribution company €12,000 for a violation of Article 5(1)(f) of the GDPR.

A supermarket customer submitted a request via Mercadona's website to access security camera footage following an accident, aiming to substantiate a damages claim. Mercadona failed to respond within one month, later claiming it had not received the request and that the recordings were erased due to an internal human error. The Spanish Data Protection Authority (AEPD) established that Mercadona breached Articles 12 and 15 GDPR by failing to handle the data subject's access request within the statutory timeframe, as well as Article 6 GDPR for unlawful processing. Rejecting Mercadona's arguments regarding early termination reductions under administrative law, the AEPD imposed fines totaling EUR 170,000 (EUR 70,000 for Articles 12/15 and EUR 100,000 for Article 6) and ordered the company to bring its practices into compliance within one month.

The Spanish DPA investigated Google LLC after complaints about Google passing personal data contained in content-removal requests to the Lumen Project website (lumendatabase.org). It found an infringement of Article 6 GDPR (no legal basis) and of Article 17 GDPR (right to erasure), and fined Google EUR 5,000,000 for each, EUR 10,000,000 in total. It also ordered Google to bring its processing operations and the procedures for exercising the right into line with data protection law within six months.

The Hungarian DPA fined a news service 2,000,000 HUF (approx. €5,080) for processing personal data without valid consent. Data subjects who signed up for the controller's newsletter were automatically signed up to electronic marketing and a prize draw without being sufficiently informed nor being able to give granular consent.
An association that disclosed personal data of one of its members in a Whatsapp group was fined €3,000 for violating Articles 5(1)(f) and 32 GDPR.

A customer complained to the Bavarian authority that Openbank, for anti-money-laundering checks, asked him to prove the origin of funds but offered no secure channel, only ordinary unencrypted email. The complaint was passed to the AEPD as lead authority. The AEPD found that Openbank had breached Article 25 GDPR (data protection by design) and Article 32 GDPR (security of processing), as its risk assessment did not cover this document collection and no secure channel existed from May 2018 to October 2022. It imposed a fine of EUR 1,500,000 for Article 25 and EUR 1,000,000 for Article 32, EUR 2,500,000 in total.

The Spanish DPA sanctioned Orange Espagne after fraudulent SIM card duplicates were issued, enabling identity theft and fraudulent banking activity. It found that Orange had processed personal data without a lawful basis (Article 6) and had not put in place data protection by design measures (Article 25). It imposed EUR 200,000 for the Article 6 infringement and EUR 1,000,000 for the Article 25 infringement, and ordered Orange to report within six months the measures taken to ensure duplicate requests come from the line holder. Orange's arguments on criminal prejudicial issues, concurrent infringements, strict liability and proportionality were rejected.

Amadeus, a global distribution system (GDS) provider for the travel industry, used travellers' booking data in a pilot project that ran from 15 March to 15 June 2022. Millions of people were affected. They were not informed as Article 14 GDPR requires, and the processing had no valid legal basis under Article 6 GDPR. The AEPD proposed a fine of EUR 9,000,000 for each infringement, EUR 18,000,000 in total. Amadeus paid voluntarily without admitting responsibility, which gave a 20% reduction to EUR 14,400,000. The proceedings ended on that payment, and Amadeus waived its administrative appeal.

A customer filed a complaint with the Spanish Data Protection Authority (AEPD) after an unauthorized third party fraudulently obtained a duplicate SIM card at a retail store. The AEPD determined that Xfera Móviles (Yoigo) acted with gross negligence by failing to follow its established identity verification procedures, thereby processing personal data without a valid legal basis under Article 6(1) GDPR. Taking into account the company's annual turnover and a previous fine for a similar SIM swapping incident, the regulator imposed a fine of EUR 200,000. Additionally, Xfera was ordered to demonstrate within six months the adoption of measures to prevent similar incidents and guarantee lawful data processing.

On 30 May 2023, Vodafone España notified the Spanish data protection authority of a personal data breach resulting from a ransomware attack on a customer service data processor. The incident compromised unencrypted MSISDNs and landline telephone numbers of 486,768 individual customers as well as contact telephone numbers of 14,571 corporate authorized representatives. The AEPD found that Vodafone failed to ensure appropriate technical and organisational security measures under Article 32 GDPR, pointing to basic security deficiencies at the processor including known unpatched vulnerabilities and lack of pre-incident encryption for phone numbers. The AEPD imposed an administrative fine of EUR 400,000 on Vodafone España.

Vodafone España notified the AEPD of a personal data breach originating from a cyberattack on a processor that provided software services for its Super Wifi 5 application. The incident exposed personal data of Vodafone customers, including email addresses and names. The AEPD found that Vodafone breached the confidentiality principle, failed to implement appropriate technical and organizational security measures, and engaged the processor without a valid data processing agreement in place at the time of the breach. The authority imposed three administrative fines totaling €750,000.

Vodafone España notified the Spanish Data Protection Authority (AEPD) of a ransomware attack affecting an IT system managed by a data processor, which compromised personal data of 724,733 customers. Although proceedings were initiated for alleged violations of both Article 5(1)(f) and Article 32 GDPR, the AEPD determined that all facts constituted a single infringement of Article 32 GDPR due to basic security deficiencies. Taking into account aggravating factors such as the number of affected individuals, serious negligence, previous sanctions, and the nature of the business, alongside post-breach mitigation measures as an attenuating factor, the AEPD imposed an administrative fine of €500,000.

The DPA fined a genomics and biotechnology company €2.4 million for failing to adequately protect sensitive genetic and health data and for notifying the DPA about a personal data breach after the 72-hour deadline.
